items.question: What happens when the vital breaths spread their wings?
premises: Prāṇa and apāna are the two vital breaths
Their wings are described as burst open
items.inference: The two breaths become active and expansive like wings.
uncertainties: Exact verbal form and root of phuṭaritha are uncertain
items.plain_english: The prāṇa and apāna breaths have burst open their wings.

items.question: How are the two vital winds brought under control?
premises: The two winds have wings that can move
Restraint obstructs those wings
items.inference: By obstructing their wings, the two breaths are restrained.
uncertainties: Whether nodena implies yogic technique or general restraint
items.plain_english: By restraint and the obstruction of their wings, the two winds are checked.

items.question: What state characterizes those who are blessed and freed from ripening bondage?
premises: The person is not cooked or ripened by bondage
The blessed ones are described as plundered
items.inference: The blessed are those stripped of binding ripeness.
uncertainties: Vernacular forms suha, tāya, lūsiti have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: He is not bound by ripening, and the blessed ones are plundered of it.

items.question: Why can no creditor claim wealth from the liberated person?
premises: The liberated person is not subject to a creditor
He is indeed debtless
items.inference: Because he is debtless, no creditor can take anything from him.
uncertainties: Sandhi in so 'nṛṇaḥ reflects elision but surface is preserved as given
items.plain_english: He is liberated; no creditor takes his wealth, for he is indeed debtless.

items.question: What can be said about consciousness dwelling in the body's forest?
premises: Consciousness is associated with the body as a forest
The question asks what can be spoken of it
items.inference: The relation of consciousness to the body defies ordinary description.
uncertainties: Vernacular kyāha and vana have uncertain exact grammatical analysis
items.plain_english: Consciousness in the forest of the body—what can one say?

items.question: Why cannot the mind be led to discrimination through thoughts of enjoyment?
premises: Discrimination is a state the mind must reach
Thoughts of enjoyment do not lead the mind there
items.inference: Preoccupation with enjoyment prevents the mind from attaining discrimination.
items.plain_english: The mind cannot be brought to discrimination by constant thoughts of enjoyment.

items.question: What quality makes innate reflection difficult to attain?
premises: Innate reflection is still present as a possibility
It is described as hard to obtain
items.inference: Even so, spontaneous innate reflection remains rare.
uncertainties: Vernacular toti and chuya have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: Even so, innate reflection is hard to obtain.

items.question: Why is innate reflection not easily obtained even upon attaining oneness?
premises: Attainment of oneness may occur
Even then this reflection is not obtainable
items.inference: Mere attainment of oneness does not guarantee innate reflection.
uncertainties: ikatāptāv shows nonstandard spelling for ekatāptau
items.plain_english: Thus, even when oneness is attained, this is not easily obtained.

items.question: What results when void merges completely with void?
premises: Void is joined with void
A merging or union takes place
items.inference: The merging of void with void yields a state of undivided emptiness.
uncertainties: Vernacular śūnyāha and gauva have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: Void united with void and became one.

rows.grounds: the idea of difference in that

items.question: Why is the notion of difference in that reality declared futile?
premises: A prior conclusion has been established
The notion of difference arises in the addressee
items.inference: Given that conclusion, holding a notion of difference is vain.
items.plain_english: Therefore, your notion of difference in that is entirely in vain.

items.question: What identity is affirmed between all, that, and the self?
premises: All is identified with that
The speaker denies being other than anyone
items.inference: All, that, and the self are not separate entities.
uncertainties: Vernacular forms soruya, suya, tāya, bvaha, nava, ke/ha are uncertain in exact parsing
items.plain_english: All is that, and I am not anyone other.

items.question: What dualities are negated in the recognition of nondual reality?
premises: The speaker negates I and you
The manifested world is also negated as separate
items.inference: Neither self, other, nor the manifested world stands as an independent reality.
items.plain_english: Not I, not you, and indeed not this manifested world.

items.question: How can some remain actionless while engaged in household life?
premises: Some are engaged in the house
They are described as actionless
items.inference: Outward household engagement does not necessarily imply binding action.
uncertainties: Vernacular ke/h, chiya, bajitha have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: Some are engaged in the house, yet remain actionless.

items.question: How can another person remain completely pure despite enjoying a woman?
premises: Another person has enjoyed a woman
That person is described as very pure
items.inference: Purity is not negated by such enjoyment in this realized state.
uncertainties: The doctrinal justification for purity amid transgression is implied, not explicit
items.plain_english: Another, even after enjoying a woman, remains completely pure.

items.question: What use are a thousand mantras performed by others for such a person?
premises: Others may perform a thousand mantras
The question challenges their usefulness for him
items.inference: External mantras performed by others are of no use to him.
uncertainties: Vernacular tasa, sāsa, mantara, kyāha, kare have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: What can a thousand mantras done by others do for him?

items.question: What can be accomplished for him by multitudes of other mantras?
premises: Other mantras exist in multitudes
Their necessity for him is questioned
items.inference: No further accomplishment is needed for him through other mantras.
items.plain_english: What is to be done for him by multitudes of other mantras?

items.question: Why are death and immortality regarded as equal in the realized view?
premises: Death and immortality are both considered
They are equal in form toward the speaker
items.inference: For the realized one, death and immortality hold the same value.
items.plain_english: To me, death and immortality are of equal form.

items.question: Whom should one worship when drink and deity are questioned?
premises: Drink and worship are mentioned
The object of worship is asked as whom
items.inference: The question challenges the need for an external object of worship.
uncertainties: Vernacular pānaya, ta, arcuna, kasa have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: Drink, god, and worship—for whom are they?

items.question: Whom would the wise person worship when the divine has become the self?
premises: The divine has become one's own self
A wise person recognizes this identity
items.inference: When the divine is the self, there is no other to worship.
items.plain_english: When that has become one's own self, whom would the wise person worship?

items.question: What visual illusion appears when seen from a distance?
premises: Something is seen from afar
It appears as running blue
items.inference: Distance creates the appearance of a spreading blue expanse.
uncertainties: Vernacular deśakha, dūryā, dramana, nīliya have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: Seen from afar, it appears as a running blue expanse.

items.question: How does the appearance of the grass ground change when seen from near?
premises: From afar it appeared blue
From near the dūrvā ground shines very blue
items.inference: Proximity reveals the true nature of what seemed different at a distance.
uncertainties: Initial r in rdūrvāsthalaṃ may reflect sandhi or scribal form
items.plain_english: From near, the dūrvā-grass ground shines intensely blue.

items.question: In what sense is the realized person not born within the world?
premises: The person is situated in the world
He is said not to be born by birth
items.inference: Though appearing in the world, he is not truly born in bondage.
uncertainties: Vernacular suha, saṃsārasa, jyayi, necha have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: He is in the world, yet not born by birth.

items.question: Why does worldly existence not afflict the realized person's fruitful life?
premises: The world does not afflict him
His life is fruitful
items.inference: Living in the world without affliction, his life attains its true fruit.
items.plain_english: The world does not afflict him, and his life is fruitful.

items.question: What is ultimately revealed about all conduct as mere artifice?
premises: All things are considered in the end
They are characterized as deceitful conduct
items.inference: Ultimately, all conduct is seen as artifice or display.
uncertainties: Vernacular antiha, sakalu, kapaṭa-caryatha have uncertain exact parsing
items.plain_english: In the end, all is deceitful conduct.
